# CMeTTa by example

Every file under [`language-feature-examples/`](language-feature-examples) is a
**twin**: one MeTTa example from
[the MeTTa corpus](https://github.com/MesTTo/MeTTa-Examples), written again in C
on [CMeTTa](https://github.com/MesTTo/CMeTTa)'s surface, at its original's
path. A twin proves every claim its original makes, and it does so with **no
MeTTa source text**, except where the text is what its original is about, as
[the list below](#where-a-twin-cannot-follow) derived from the twins says.
Terms are built with cmetta's constructors, a computation the host can own is
a C function the engine calls, and each claim is a C check on what the engine
answers. So a pair answers a question prose cannot: given a
thing MeTTa says one way, what does C say?

Each section below is a real pair, the MeTTa original above and its C twin
underneath, shortest twin first. The C is the twin's file verbatim with only
its obligation header cut, and the original loses only its comments. `make
index` copies both from the files, so a pair cannot drift from what the lane
runs.

Beside the twins, `basics/`, `data/`, `gallery/`, `integration/`, `live/`,
`operations/` and `reasoning/` hold C programs about embedding the engine:
ownership, callbacks, threads, SQLite and BLAS. [INDEX.md](INDEX.md) lists
every program and what it proves.

## Many answers are a C list

<!-- pair: ch06-many-answers/03-collapse -->
```metta
!(test (collapse (1 2 3))
       ((1 2 3)))
```

```c
#define MT_SHORTHAND
#include "common.h"

int main(void)
{
    metta *m = open_engine();
    check_list("(1 2 3) answers itself, once", mt_all(mt_eval(m, E(1, 2, 3))), E(1, 2, 3));
    return done(m);
}
```
<!-- pair:end -->

A MeTTa call answers any number of answers, and `mt_eval` hands them back as a
cursor. `collapse` is `mt_all`, every answer gathered into one C list, and
`check_list` holds that list to what it must be. `E(1, 2, 3)` builds the
expression `(1 2 3)` with each child coerced by its C type, so no string is
parsed on the way. `open_engine()` and `done()` open and close the runtime,
and `done()` also reports what the lane compares with the original.

## A recursive definition with a budget

<!-- pair: ch22-a-reasoner-you-can-serve/22-03-search/05-fibadd -->
```metta
!(add-atom &self (= (fib $N)
                    (if (< $N 2)
                        $N
                        (+ (fib (- $N 1))
                           (fib (- $N 2))))))

!(test (with-pragma! ((max-stack-depth 100000000)) (fib 30)) 832040)
```

```c
#define MT_SHORTHAND
#include "common.h"
#include "../../ch07-control-flow/07-05-recursion/fib.h"

int main(void)
{
    metta *m = open_engine();
    require("add the equation", mt_add(m, fib_equation()));
    check_answers("fib 30 under the budget", mt_eval(m, E("with-pragma!", E(E("max-stack-depth", 100000000)), E("fib", 30))), fib(30));
    return done(m);
}
```
<!-- pair:end -->

[`fib.h`](language-feature-examples/ch07-control-flow/07-05-recursion/fib.h)
holds `FIB`, one body over `lowering.h`'s operators: with C's it is the
recursive C function `fib()`, with the atom builders it is the equation
`fib_equation()` returns. The twin adds that atom with `mt_add`, the space's
own door, as the original adds it with `add-atom`, and the value the engine
answers at 30 must be the C function's. The pragma is a term like any other.

## Types, and reading a type back

<!-- pair: ch09-types/08-parametric_types -->
```metta
(: apply (-> (-> $tx $ty) $tx $ty))
(= (apply $f $x) ($f $x))
!(apply not False)
!(get-type (apply not False))
!(test (let (get-type apply) (-> (-> Bool Bool) Bool $result) $result)
       Bool)
```

```c
#define MT_SHORTHAND
#include "common.h"

int main(void)
{
    metta *m = open_engine();
    require("(: apply (-> (-> $tx $ty) $tx $ty))", mt_add(m, E(":", "apply", E("->", E("->", V("tx"), V("ty")), V("tx"), V("ty")))));
    require("(= (apply $f $x) ($f $x))", mt_add(m, E("=", E("apply", V("f"), V("x")), E(V("f"), V("x")))));
    check_answers("apply runs not", mt_eval(m, E("apply", "not", B(false))), B(!false));
    check_answers("its type is not's result", mt_eval(m, E("get-type", E("apply", "not", B(false)))), S("Bool"));
    check_answers("$result unifies to Bool",
                  mt_eval(m, E("let", E("get-type", "apply"), E("->", E("->", "Bool", "Bool"), "Bool", V("result")), V("result"))), S("Bool"));
    return done(m);
}
```
<!-- pair:end -->

A type is a term: `(-> (-> $tx $ty) $tx $ty)` is built with `E` and `V` and
added with `mt_add`. `B(false)` is MeTTa's `False`, which a C `bool` passed
to `E` would not be, since C promotes it to an integer first. The last claim
asks the engine to unify apply's type with a pattern and answer the binding,
which is `Bool` whichever of the two C builds.

## An equation is a function

<!-- pair: ch05-equations-and-evaluation/05-01-an-equation-is-a-rewrite/01-identity -->
```metta
(= (f $x) (* $x $x))

!(test (f 1) 1)
```

```c
#define MT_SHORTHAND
#include "common.h"
#include "lowering.h"

/* One body, two languages: MUL is C's * in one expansion and the atom
   (* a b) in the other, so the definition cannot say two different things. */
#define SQUARE(MUL, x) MUL(x, x)

static int64_t square(int64_t x) { return SQUARE(C_MUL, x); }

int main(void)
{
    metta *m = open_engine();
    require("define f", mt_add(m, E("=", E("f", V("x")), SQUARE(T_MUL, V("x")))));

    check_int("(f 1) is 1", mt_one_int(mt_eval(m, E("f", 1))), 1);

    bool agree = true;
    for (int64_t x = -100; x <= 100 && agree; x++)
        agree = mt_one_int(mt_eval(m, E("f", x))) == square(x);
    check("the equation computes square() on -100..100", agree);
    return done(m);
}
```
<!-- pair:end -->

`SQUARE` is written once over its operator. With `lowering.h`'s `C_MUL` it is
the C function `square()`, and with `T_MUL`, which builds the atom `(* a b)`,
it is the body of the equation `mt_add` installs, `(= (f $x) (* $x $x))`, so
the program the engine runs and the function C checks it against cannot say
two different things. The equation is built as an atom, so no text is written
or read on the way. `mt_one_int` takes the answer as a C integer and claims
there is exactly one.

## C is a host, not a foreign country

<!-- pair: ch19-spaces-backed-by-anything/19-03-a-builtin-in-c/01-c_extension -->
```metta
!(import! &self (library lib_import))
!(import! &self (library lib_file))

!(if (file-exists "./examples/ch19-spaces-backed-by-anything/19-03-a-builtin-in-c/cbump.so")
     (import_prolog_functions_from_file
        "./examples/ch19-spaces-backed-by-anything/19-03-a-builtin-in-c/loader.pl" (c-bump))
     (println! "SKIPPED c_extension: cbump.so is not built, see the README beside this file"))

!(if (file-exists "./examples/ch19-spaces-backed-by-anything/19-03-a-builtin-in-c/cbump.so")
     (test (eval (c-bump 41)) 42)
     True)
```

```c
#define MT_SHORTHAND
#include "common.h"
#include "lowering.h"

#define BUMP(ADD, x) ADD(x, 1)

static mt_status c_bump(mt_call *call, void *user)
{
    (void)user;
    if (mt_kind_of(mt_arg(call, 0)) != MT_INT) return MT_FAIL;
    return mt_answer(call, N(BUMP(C_ADD, mt_int(mt_arg(call, 0)))));
}

int main(void)
{
    metta *m = open_engine();
    /* The original's own imports: its loader needs lib_import and its guard
       lib_file, and C needs neither, but &self holds what they define on
       both sides. */
    static const char *const libraries[] = { "lib_import", "lib_file" };
    for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof libraries / sizeof *libraries; i++)
        require(libraries[i], mt_one_truth(mt_eval(m, E("import!", "&self", E("library", libraries[i])))));
    require("c-bump", mt_def(m, (mt_op){ .name = "c-bump", .arity = 1, .effect = MT_EFFECT_CLASS_PURE_STRUCTURAL, .fn = c_bump }));
    check_answers("(c-bump 41) is C's", mt_eval(m, E("c-bump", 41)), BUMP(C_ADD, 41));
    return done(m);
}
```
<!-- pair:end -->

The original compiles a foreign predicate against SWI-Prolog and loads it
through a Prolog loader. In C there is nothing to load: `c_bump` is a C
function, `mt_def` publishes it under its MeTTa name with its arity and its
effect class, and the engine calls it with nothing in between. A function reads
its arguments with `mt_arg`, answers with `mt_answer`, and says it does not
apply with `MT_FAIL`. The embedding examples go further: callbacks that
answer many times, spaces backed by C stores, threads attached to one
runtime, and SQLite and BLAS behind MeTTa functions.

## A pattern selects on shape, not on names

<!-- pair: ch04-spaces-and-matching/04-02-patterns-and-bindings/05-constanthead -->
```metta
(= (h (justdata haha $B) $C)
   (+ $B $C))

!(test (h (justdata haha 30) 40) 70)
```

```c
#define MT_SHORTHAND
#include "common.h"

static bool is_symbol(const mt_atom *atom, const char *name)
{
    return mt_kind_of(atom) == MT_SYMBOL && strcmp(mt_name(atom), name) == 0;
}

static mt_status h(mt_call *call, void *user)
{
    (void)user;
    const mt_atom *data = mt_arg(call, 0);
    if (mt_len(data) != 3 || !is_symbol(mt_at(data, 0), "justdata") ||
        !is_symbol(mt_at(data, 1), "haha"))
        return MT_FAIL;                     /* not this shape: no answer */
    mt_clear();
    int64_t b = mt_int(mt_at(data, 2)), c = mt_int(mt_arg(call, 1));
    if (!mt_ok()) return mt_fail(call, "h adds two integers");
    return mt_answer(call, N(b + c));
}

int main(void)
{
    metta *m = open_engine();
    require("publish h", mt_def(m, (mt_op){ .name = "h", .arity = 2, .effect = MT_EFFECT_CLASS_PURE_STRUCTURAL, .fn = h }));
    check_int("(h (justdata haha 30) 40) is 70",
              mt_one_int(mt_eval(m, E("h", E("justdata", "haha", 30), 40))), 70);
    return done(m);
}
```
<!-- pair:end -->

The head pattern becomes a C function that reads its first argument's shape
with `mt_len`, `mt_at` and `mt_kind_of`. A shape it does not take answers
`MT_FAIL`, which is no match, as the original's head matches nothing else.
Ownership is explicit throughout: `mt_arg` and `mt_at` borrow, `N` and `E`
make atoms the call that receives them takes, and a status is checked where
the door returns one.

## Running them

You need a C11 compiler, Make, Python 3, pkg-config, the development files
of the C libraries the programs link (SQLite, OpenBLAS, PCRE2, cJSON,
OpenSSL's libcrypto and GMP, each found through pkg-config), and the patched
SWI-Prolog 10 the engine runs on, first on your `PATH`. The engine refuses a
stock SWI-Prolog when it boots, and
[docs/patched-host.md](https://github.com/MesTTo/MeTTa/blob/main/docs/patched-host.md)
shows how to build and declare the patched one. Clone MeTTa beside this
repository: its `examples/` are the originals the twins are held against, and
its `extensions/cmetta` is the C surface.

```sh
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/MesTTo/MeTTa.git ../MeTTa
make surface
make -j8 all
make check JOBS=4
make check-consumers
```

For a MeTTa checkout elsewhere, name it and its C component:

```sh
make check CMETTA_ENGINE=$HOME/src/MeTTa CMETTA_DIR=$HOME/src/MeTTa/extensions/cmetta
```

`make check` runs the embedding examples, then the twin lane,
[`tools/twin_lane.py`](tools/twin_lane.py), which runs every original through
the C seat and every twin in its own process and compares what they answer:
the claims each proves, the definitions each makes visible, and the atoms each
leaves in `&self`. It also reads each program's translation unit, which `make
all` writes beside the binary as the compiler sees it, for MeTTa source handed
to the engine: a cmetta door that reads source or runs a file, taken from
`cmetta.h` itself, and a head such as `parse` that reads its string as MeTTa.
A macro cannot hide one, since the unit holds what the macro expanded to, and
only a file with a `text:` note may use one. `make twins
TWIN=language-feature-examples/ch03-atoms-and-expressions` runs the lane over
part of the corpus, and `tools/twin_lane_selftest.py` proves the lane refuses a
twin that drifts or hands the engine text.

`common.h` holds the checks every program states its claims through:
`check`, `check_int`, `check_text`, `check_atom` and `check_answers` are
claims, and `require` is a status the program needs before it can go on.
A false claim exits nonzero whatever `NDEBUG` says. `open_engine()` gives
cmetta a counting allocator, and `done()` refuses a program that leaves any
atom it made unreleased once the engine has closed, so ownership as
`cmetta.h` prescribes it is checked, not assumed.

## Reading order

Directory names are the reading order, so a listing is the index:

```text
ch07-control-flow/07-02-case/03-caseconstrain.c
^chapter          ^section   ^order within the section
```

Chapter and section numbers match the MeTTa corpus exactly, so
`ch07-control-flow/07-02-case/03-caseconstrain.c` is the twin of
`examples/ch07-control-flow/07-02-case/03-caseconstrain.metta`. Read them side
by side, with the Python seat's twin of the same original beside them for a
third way of saying it. A header beside the twins of one section, such as
`ch22-a-reasoner-you-can-serve/22-02-weighted-answers/nars_truth.h`, is the C
model those twins share, and `lowering.h`, `verdicts.h` and `common.h` at the
root serve the whole corpus.

**If you are an LLM, read cmetta's
[llms.txt](https://github.com/MesTTo/CMeTTa/blob/main/llms.txt)** for the whole
surface with exact ownership and return shapes, rather than inferring it from
here.

Chapters 1, 2, 13 and 21 of the MeTTa corpus are installation, a first
program, the shell and the TypeScript seat, and the Python seat twins none of
their examples. Across the rest, the twins teach this C:

- **Atoms and spaces** (3, 4): the constructors, a space's writes and what a
  later match sees, and a pattern's shape selecting.
- **Equations** (5, 6, 7): one body built as an equation and compiled to C,
  many answers as a cursor, and control as the terms the engine runs.
- **Data** (8): lists and folds as C loops, sequence variables, and each
  shipped library held to the C library that does its job.
- **Types and errors** (9, 10, 12): types as terms, refusals as data, and
  the assertion family's answer bags built in C.
- **The host** (11, 14 to 17): the seam from C, transactions and hooks,
  events, and threads attached to one runtime.
- **Scale** (18): loaders that batch their atoms, and memo and table reports
  built from C's own counts.
- **Extension** (19, 20): C spaces behind providers, C builtins, the
  translator's cost model, Prolog underneath, and the module system.
- **Reasoning** (22): logic programs and tagged fixpoints, the NARS and PLN
  truth functions and derivation loop as C models, and search.

## Where a twin cannot follow

A twin never fakes what it cannot say. What C cannot say goes in
[`residue.json`](language-feature-examples/residue.json), naming the missing
spelling and the work it waits on, and what a twin does differently it
declares where the lane reads it. This list is derived from both:

<!-- follow:begin -->
- Nothing untwinned and no claim declined: [residue.json](language-feature-examples/residue.json) is empty.

Twins whose stored atoms differ from their original's as they declare, each difference pinned by its digest (2):

- [ch20-extending-the-engine/20-04-modules-and-the-catalog/12-reference_maps.c](language-feature-examples/ch20-extending-the-engine/20-04-modules-and-the-catalog/12-reference_maps.c): `9174f80e4789e79a`, the original names its fixture relative to its own file, ./_fixtures/references/...; a C program has no importing file, so it names the same fixture from the engine tree where the twin runs, and each (from ...) row it stores spells that path.
- [ch20-extending-the-engine/20-04-modules-and-the-catalog/13-reference_loading.c](language-feature-examples/ch20-extending-the-engine/20-04-modules-and-the-catalog/13-reference_loading.c): `dc6887a5e38833a7`, the original names its fixture relative to its own file, ./_fixtures/references/...; a C program has no importing file, so it names the same fixture from the engine tree where the twin runs, and each (from ...) row it stores spells that path.

Twins that read or run MeTTa text, because their original's subject is text (8):

- [ch03-atoms-and-expressions/03-string_comments.c](language-feature-examples/ch03-atoms-and-expressions/03-string_comments.c): the original tests the MeTTa reader on string literals and comments, which is source text by definition.
- [ch03-atoms-and-expressions/04-repr.c](language-feature-examples/ch03-atoms-and-expressions/04-repr.c): the original's subject is the text each atom prints as, so the expected outputs are written as text.
- [ch03-atoms-and-expressions/05-parse.c](language-feature-examples/ch03-atoms-and-expressions/05-parse.c): the original is about parse, whose input is MeTTa source.
- [ch03-atoms-and-expressions/06-reading_forms.c](language-feature-examples/ch03-atoms-and-expressions/06-reading_forms.c): the original's subject is source text a console receives, handed to parse-command and sread as data.
- [ch08-data/08-03-the-shipped-libraries/27-parsing_lib.c](language-feature-examples/ch08-data/08-03-the-shipped-libraries/27-parsing_lib.c): lib_parsing's subject is text a grammar reads, so the inputs C hands it, "(1+2)" among them, are arithmetic text, never MeTTa forms.
- [ch08-data/08-03-the-shipped-libraries/42-database_lib.c](language-feature-examples/ch08-data/08-03-the-shipped-libraries/42-database_lib.c): a row keeps a value as its MeTTa source, written by mt_write_dup and read back by mt_parsen, so a text holding NUL survives; a store keeping syntax in a file keeps it as text.
- [ch08-data/08-03-the-shipped-libraries/44-cli_lib.c](language-feature-examples/ch08-data/08-03-the-shipped-libraries/44-cli_lib.c): the metta type reads one MeTTa form from its token with mt_parsen, which is what the library's type does.
- [ch20-extending-the-engine/20-07-tokens-and-the-reader/01-reader-tokens.c](language-feature-examples/ch20-extending-the-engine/20-07-tokens-and-the-reader/01-reader-tokens.c): the original is about what the reader builds from text, so C reads the text it builds through mt_parse, the engine's own reader.
<!-- follow:end -->
